entry.title: What Tools Integrate Gen AI With Web Applications?
entry.summary: Integrating Generative AI (Gen AI) with web applications involves using a variety of tools and frameworks that simplify development and deployment. One of the most common methods is through APIs like OpenAI’s GPT models, which allow developers to send prompts and receive text-based responses. These APIs can be easily integrated using JavaScript, Python (Flask, Django), or Node.js backends. For front-end support, tools like React or Vue.js often serve as the interface layer interacting with AI backends. Frameworks such as LangChain or LlamaIndex help manage complex chains of AI prompts and responses, useful for building more advanced applications like AI assistants or chatbots. Serverless platforms like Vercel, Firebase, or AWS Lambda are also frequently used to deploy Gen AI-powered services efficiently. For visual outputs, tools like Stability AI or RunwayML enable image generation within browser environments. Additionally, tools like Hugging Face Transformers offer a wide range of pre-trained models that can be fine-tuned for specific tasks in web environments. These integrations enable developers to add intelligent features like content generation, summarization, and personalization to websites and web apps effectively. To learn more, consider a Generative AI online course.

entry.title: C++, Unsafe Doesn’t Always Mean Dangerous : How I increased performance with raw pointers
entry.summary:
TL;DR:
When building a real-time video rendering and encoding pipeline in C++, I hit a surprising bottleneck: memory allocation. Despite using high-performance libraries like OpenGL and FFmpeg, the cost of safely copying ~5MB per frame killed my frame budget. The fix? Using raw pointers with a manually managed double buffer. It’s not idiomatic C++, but in this case, “unsafe” code—done carefully—was the only way to hit performance targets. As a person who worked in managed runtimes like NodeJs and the Golang runtime, thinking about memory management always felt like premature optimisations because the runtime, or the underlying libraries generally handled it really well. However, in C++ it is the name of the game. The language offers multiple ways to manage memory and resource lifecycles …
